cards.heading: ES modules are a singleton for free
cards.hook: Export an object from a module and Node's module cache guarantees every importer gets the exact same instance — the simplest singleton you'll ever write.
cards.code: export default pool; // same pool instance everywhere it's imported

cards.heading: The class-based singleton shape
cards.hook: A private static #instance field, plus a constructor that returns the existing instance instead of creating a new one, is the whole pattern.

cards.heading: Singleton vs a global variable
cards.hook: A singleton is lazily created and accessed through a controlled getInstance() — a global variable is just always-allocated state nobody controls.

cards.heading: The usual singleton suspects in a backend
cards.hook: DB connection pools, config, loggers, and cache clients are singletons in nearly every real backend — expensive to set up once, shared everywhere after.

cards.heading: An event bus singleton decouples publishers from subscribers
cards.hook: A single shared EventEmitter instance lets completely unrelated files publish and subscribe to the same events without importing each other.
cards.body: orderService emits ORDER_PLACED; emailService and analyticsService each subscribe independently.

cards.heading: A Redis client singleton centralizes connection lifecycle
cards.hook: One RedisClient class with a private #instance handles connect, get, set, and del — every file that needs caching imports the same already-connected client.

cards.heading: Singletons fight testing on purpose
cards.hook: Shared global state is the whole point of a singleton, which is exactly what makes it hard to reset between tests.
cards.body: Inject it as a constructor dependency instead of importing it directly, and tests can swap in a mock.

cards.heading: A test-only reset escape hatch
cards.hook: A static _reset() method, gated behind NODE_ENV === 'test', lets test suites clear a singleton's cached instance between runs without touching production code paths.

cards.heading: When singleton is the wrong call
cards.hook: If the only-one-instance requirement is artificial, or it's just making tests harder, you don't have a singleton problem — you built one you didn't need.

cards.heading: Prefer the module cache over custom getInstance()
cards.hook: In Node.js, exporting an already-created instance is simpler than writing a getInstance() class — reach for the class version only when you need lazy init.

cards.heading: Private class fields make a singleton tamper-proof
cards.hook: A #instance field declared with the # syntax genuinely can't be reached from outside the class — nothing external can quietly create a second instance.

cards.heading: A factory hides which class actually gets built
cards.hook: The caller just says createNotification('email') — it never needs to know EmailNotification exists as a class.

cards.heading: A map beats a switch for a factory
cards.hook: A plain object mapping type to class scales better than a switch statement — adding a new type means adding one line, not touching the factory function.

cards.heading: Factory Method lets subclasses decide
cards.hook: A base class defines an abstract createLogger() step, and each subclass overrides it — DevelopmentLoggerFactory returns a console logger, ProductionLoggerFactory returns a cloud one.

cards.heading: Open registration makes a factory pluggable
cards.hook: A factory with a register(type, Class) method lets any module add a new type at runtime — the factory never needs to know every type upfront.

cards.heading: Factory answers creation, Strategy answers behavior
cards.hook: Factory decides which object to create; Strategy decides how that object behaves — in real apps they're almost always used together.
cards.code:
const strategy = carrierFactory.create(carrier); // Factory
await strategy.createShipment(order);              // Strategy

cards.heading: A factory can pick a database client by environment variable
cards.hook: createDbClient(process.env.DB_TYPE) swaps between PostgresClient and MongoClient with one line — the rest of the app never branches on database type.

cards.heading: One route, three export formats, one factory
cards.hook: createReportGenerator(req.query.format) returns a CSV, JSON, or PDF generator from the exact same Express route handler.

cards.heading: A mock factory makes a whole consumer testable in one line
cards.hook: const mockFactory = { create: () => ({ send: jest.fn() }) } swaps in for the real factory, and everything that uses it becomes instantly test-safe.

cards.heading: Skip the factory for one concrete class
cards.hook: If you only ever create one type of object, a factory adds indirection for no benefit — just call new directly.

cards.heading: A factory centralizes creation logic in one place
cards.hook: Every rule about which concrete class to build lives in one function instead of being copy-pasted at every call site — change the rule once, not everywhere.

cards.heading: Strategy replaces if/else chains with interchangeable objects
cards.hook: Multiple ways to do the same job, each behind the same interface, chosen at runtime instead of branching on a type string.

cards.heading: Plain functions can be strategies too
cards.hook: In JS a strategy doesn't need a class — flatDiscount(200) returning a function that takes a price is the shortest, most idiomatic version.

cards.heading: Swap a strategy at runtime, not just at startup
cards.hook: A context object holds a reference to its current strategy and exposes setStrategy() — the same calculator can switch from no-discount to percentage-discount mid-run.

cards.heading: Strategy is how you add a payment method without touching checkout
cards.hook: A new RazorpayStrategy or StripeStrategy just implements pay(amount) — PaymentService never changes.

cards.heading: Factory and Strategy are almost always paired in production
cards.hook: getCarrierStrategy(carrier) picks the right shipping strategy, then carrierService.createShipment(order) runs it — one Factory call, one Strategy call, completely decoupled.

cards.heading: Strategy is Open/Closed in practice
cards.hook: Adding a FestivalDiscountStrategy for a 30% off sale means writing one new class — zero lines of existing discount logic touched or re-tested.

cards.heading: Class strategies for state, function strategies for stateless transforms
cards.hook: A strategy that only transforms input to output is a plain function; one that needs to remember configuration, like a discount amount, is cleaner as a small class.

cards.heading: Don't build a strategy for one or two conditions
cards.hook: Twelve classes to express an if/else with two branches is design-pattern cosplay, not good architecture.

cards.heading: The tell that code wants to become a Strategy
cards.hook: A switch statement branching on provider, country, or tenant is almost always a Strategy pattern wearing a disguise.

cards.heading: A subject notifies observers automatically
cards.hook: The subject doesn't call each subscriber by name — it just notifies its list, and every subscriber reacts independently.

cards.heading: EventEmitter is Observer, built into Node.js
cards.hook: Every time you call .on() in Node.js, you're using the Observer pattern — it's not a library feature, it's the pattern itself.

cards.heading: One event, many independent reactions
cards.hook: USER_REGISTERED can trigger a welcome email, a free trial, a CRM contact, and an analytics event — each owned by its own listener, none aware of the others.

cards.heading: once() for events that should only fire a single time
cards.hook: A handler registered with .once() auto-removes itself after firing — perfect for a first-order celebration email or a one-time init hook.

cards.heading: Observer is loose coupling by design
cards.hook: The subject never knows what its observers do, or how many there are — add or remove one without touching the subject at all.

cards.heading: A typed EventEmitter wrapper kills magic strings
cards.hook: Wrapping EventEmitter with onOrderShipped(handler) and emitOrderShipped(id) methods gives you autocomplete-friendly event names instead of guessing string literals everywhere.

cards.heading: One low-stock event reaches two unrelated systems
cards.hook: A LOW_STOCK event fires once, and Slack gets an alert while procurement raises a reorder — InventoryService never calls either system directly.

cards.heading: Observer fans a database write out to every WebSocket client
cards.hook: One RECORD_UPDATED event fires after a DB write, and a single observer broadcasts it to every open connection — the write logic never touches networking code.

cards.heading: removeListener cleans up observers you no longer need
cards.hook: orderService.off('ORDER_STATUS_CHANGED', auditHandler) detaches one specific handler without touching any of the others still subscribed.

cards.heading: When Observer makes debugging harder, not easier
cards.hook: A chain of notifications that's hard to trace, or observers that must fire in a strict guaranteed order, is a sign Observer is the wrong tool here.

cards.heading: The question that reveals a hidden Observer
cards.hook: sendEmail(order); sendSms(order); updateInventory(order); all tightly coupled in one function — should this become an event instead?

cards.heading: A decorator wraps a function without touching it
cards.hook: withLogging(getUser) returns a brand new function that logs before and after calling the original — getUser itself never changes.

cards.heading: Stack decorators to build complex behavior from simple parts
cards.hook: Logging, caching, retry, and timing can all wrap the same function at once — each decorator does exactly one thing.

cards.heading: A Proxy can decorate every method of an object at once
cards.hook: Wrap a whole service in a Proxy that intercepts every property access, and you get logging on every method without touching any of them individually.

cards.heading: Decorator is how you add auth without polluting business logic
cards.hook: requireRole('admin', deleteUser) wraps the handler with a permission check — deleteUser itself stays pure business logic.

cards.heading: Test the core function and each decorator separately
cards.hook: processOrder gets tested with zero logging or retry noise, and withRetry gets tested in total isolation against a fake flaky function.

cards.heading: A rate-limit decorator tracks state the wrapped function never sees
cards.hook: withRateLimit keeps a per-user call log in a closure — the original function stays completely unaware that throttling exists.

cards.heading: Decorating a class method means reassigning it in the constructor
cards.hook: Without a transpiler, this.getUser = withCache(withLogging(this.getUser.bind(this))) inside the constructor is how you decorate instance methods in plain JS.

cards.heading: Too many wrapper layers wreck your stack traces
cards.hook: Decorator composability has a real cost — four layers deep, a thrown error's stack trace becomes much harder to read.

cards.heading: Middleware is Chain of Responsibility, running on every request
cards.hook: Each handler in the chain can act on the request, modify it, or stop it entirely — that's the whole mechanism behind every app.use() call.

cards.heading: next() is the entire contract
cards.hook: Forget to call next() and the chain just stops there — that's not a bug, it's the deliberate short-circuit mechanism middleware is built on.

cards.heading: Error middleware is detected by its argument count
cards.hook: Express looks at a middleware function's four-argument signature — err, req, res, next — to know it's an error handler, not a regular one.

cards.heading: Async handlers need an explicit error wrapper
cards.hook: A thrown error inside an async handler doesn't automatically reach next() — wrap it so a rejected promise gets forwarded to the error handler instead of hanging.

cards.heading: Middleware isn't just for HTTP
cards.hook: A job queue pipeline, an event processing pipeline, a CSV import — anything with a fixed sequence of independent steps can use the exact same pipeline shape.

cards.heading: Error handling middleware goes last
cards.hook: Register the error handler after every route, not before — middleware only catches errors from handlers registered ahead of it in the chain.

cards.heading: Each middleware is testable completely alone
cards.hook: authenticate(req, res, next) can be tested with a fake req, res, and next — zero HTTP server required.

cards.heading: Role-based authorization is just one more link in the chain
cards.hook: authorize('admin', 'manager') returns a middleware closed over the allowed roles — stack it after authenticate and the route handler never checks permissions itself.

cards.heading: A validation middleware replaces req.body with the sanitized version
cards.hook: validate(schema) doesn't just check the body — on success it reassigns req.body to the validated value, so every handler downstream can trust it.

cards.heading: Rate limiting needs per-key state, not global state
cards.hook: A Map keyed by user id or IP, each tracking its own count and reset time, is what makes one rate limiter function serve every caller independently.

cards.heading: A pipeline is just an index and a recursive next()
cards.hook: A generic middleware runner is barely ten lines: track an index, call the current middleware with a next() that advances it — the exact mechanism Express is built on, stripped to its core.

cards.heading: A repository hides which database you're even using
cards.hook: The service just asks orderRepo.findById(id) — it has zero idea whether that's hitting Postgres, Mongo, or an in-memory map.

cards.heading: An in-memory repository makes unit tests fast and real-DB-free
cards.hook: Swap in an InMemoryOrderRepository for tests, and you get pure logic tests with no database setup, no mocking framework, no fixtures.

cards.heading: Repository pays off only when queries have real complexity
cards.hook: If every repository method is a one-line passthrough to an ORM call, you're not abstracting anything — you've just added a file.

cards.heading: A caching repository wraps another repository
cards.hook: CachedOrderRepository takes a real repository in its constructor and adds a cache check in front of findById — this is Decorator applied directly to Repository.

cards.heading: Repository lets you migrate databases without touching services
cards.hook: Writing a new MongoOrderRepository that implements the same contract as the Postgres one means the service layer doesn't change a single line.

cards.heading: Skip Repository if your ORM already gives you the abstraction
cards.hook: A modern ORM like Prisma already provides a swappable, testable data layer — adding a Repository on top can just be a thin wrapper that adds no value.

cards.heading: A repository contract is just a shared method signature
cards.hook: findById, findByUserId, create, update, delete — any class implementing these five methods can stand in for the real repository, no interface required.

cards.heading: Repository keeps every query for one entity in one file
cards.hook: All the SQL that touches orders lives in PostgresOrderRepository — easy to audit, easy to index, easy to find when something's slow.

cards.heading: Patterns cluster by domain, they don't spread evenly
cards.hook: A payments team leans on Strategy and Factory constantly and barely touches Decorator; a game studio lives inside Singleton and Observer.

cards.heading: Pub/sub is Observer running across machines
cards.hook: Kafka topics, RabbitMQ exchanges, and SNS/SQS fan-out are textbook Observer — the only difference from the version you write in one process is the network in between.

cards.heading: React's state is Observer wearing a different name
cards.hook: React's hooks, Vue's reactivity, Angular's EventEmitter, and RxJS observables all solve the exact same problem Observer solves: keeping a view in sync with changing state.

cards.heading: Every pattern has an industry-specific alias
cards.hook: Strategy is called a policy in fintech, an algorithm in ML, a rule in pricing engines, and a behavior in game AI — recognizing the pattern under the vocabulary matters more than the GoF name.

cards.heading: Middleware and Decorator overlap more than people admit
cards.hook: An HTTP framework's middleware and a function decorator solve the same problem — wrapping behavior around something without changing it — just at different granularities.

cards.heading: A payments checkout stacks four patterns at once
cards.hook: Strategy picks the payment method, Factory builds the gateway client, Observer fans the order-status webhook out to email and SMS, and Decorator layers tax and coupons on the base price.

cards.heading: Naming a real product beats a hypothetical in an interview
cards.hook: Strategy, like scikit-learn swapping estimators behind .fit()/.predict(), signals you've actually seen the pattern in the wild, not just implemented the tutorial version once.

cards.heading: Builder and Adapter show up constantly without a dedicated page
cards.hook: Wrapping a third-party SDK behind the interface your app actually wants is Adapter; assembling a complex object step by step instead of a ten-parameter constructor is Builder.

cards.heading: Database connection pools are Singleton everywhere on the matrix
cards.hook: Web backends, data access layers, cloud SDKs, fintech ledgers — the one pattern that appears almost everywhere is a single, shared connection nobody duplicates.

cards.heading: Gaming's Singleton overuse is a known anti-pattern
cards.hook: GameManager, AudioManager, and InputManager singletons are so standard in Unity they're a convention — and just as commonly a source of tech debt when every system becomes one.
